text.p: President Ernesto Samper threw his weight on Tuesday behind a growing chorus of calls for an end to Colombia's constitutional ban on the extradition of drug lords and other criminals.

In an open letter to the National Council on Criminal Policy, a high-level committee responsible for shaping penal legislation, Samper said he would propose a law aimed at lifting the six-year-old ban to an upcoming session of Congress.

His letter did not specify how soon the draft law would be presented, but Samper also indicated he would support possible moves to apply extradition retroactively. If he does, and Congress approves, it could ultimately clear the way for jailed leaders of of the powerful Cali drug cartel to be tried in the United States where they are wanted on multiple drug and criminal conspiracy charges.

Colombia was notified by Washington in February that it was being kept on a U.S. drugs blacklist for a second consecutive year because of its alleged failure to prove itself a trustworthy ally in the war on drugs.

The move was widely seen as a swipe at Samper because of continuing allegations that he financed his 1994 election campaign with drug money rather than at police and military officials on the frontline of Colombia's fight against drugs, however.

In a speech to a meeting of U.S. and Colombian oil industry officials on Monday, U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette said Colombia's so-called "decertification" would be reviewed later this year and strongly hinted it could be reversed if it took certain steps to beef up its anti-drug fight.
U.S. officials have said extradition was one such step that would be applauded by Washington.

Public opinion polls taken over the last year indicate that an overwhelming majority of Colombians oppose extradition. Apart from nationalistic pride, analysts say grassroots opposition to extradition is due largely to the campaign of bombings, assassinations and kidnappings that Medellin-based drug lords led waged against the practice in the 1980s and early 1990s.

"Painful images of the years when the word extradition was synonymous with death, suffering and the anguish of thousands of inncocent people are still fresh in the minds of many Colombians," Samper said.

He added, however, that it was likely, as Justice Minister Carlos Medellin and other prominent supporters of extradition have argued in recent months, that circumstances had changed since Colombia's constituent assembly banned extradition under itense pressure from the Medellin cartel in 1991.
